📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Home » Altcoins » Solana (SOL) » GTA VI Launch Sparks $250M Solana Stock Frenzy Over Nvidia.

Tokenized Take-Two shares saw a massive 24-hour trading spike as on-chain markets attract Washington scrutiny.

The long-awaited release of Grand Theft Auto VI didn’t just break gaming records—it briefly turned publisher Take-Two Interactive into the hottest stock on the blockchain, outselling even AI giant Nvidia.

On November 18, decentralized exchange (DEX) trading volume for tokenized Take-Two shares (TTWO) exploded by 578%, jumping from $36.8 million to $249.5 million in a single day, according to Token Terminal data.

That was roughly 2.8 times the $88.1 million traded in tokenized Nvidia (NVDA) shares over the same 24-hour window, accounting for 42% of all on-chain stock trading.

Nearly all of the action, roughly $239 million, or 96% of total volume, happened on Solana via Backpack Securities, a subsidiary of crypto exchange Backpack. Debuted earlier this year, the token is designed to be backed 1:1 by real Take-Two shares held in custody.

Traditional Wall Street traders saw a much calmer reaction: Take-Two’s Nasdaq shares rose 6.2% to close at $216.61 on launch day before pulling back 3.7% to $208.65 the next session.

Despite Take-Two’s one-day viral spike, Nvidia remains the undisputed heavyweight of tokenized equities, boasting a $399.4 million market cap and $2 billion in 30-day trading volume (compared to Take-Two’s $808.1 million).

Overall, tokenized public stocks on Solana have nearly doubled since late October to reach $1.22 billion.

Sources indicate that that rapid growth is drawing fresh scrutiny in Washington. On November 16, four Democratic senators sent a letter to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) questioning how its newly introduced exemption for tokenized securities would address investor protection and anti-money laundering requirements.

According to recent reports, the issue also surfaced during the November 19 Senate Banking Committee confirmation hearing for Kristin Johnson, President Donald Trump’s nominee for the SEC. Johnson indicated that exemptions covering tokenized stocks should eventually be formalized through rules following a public comment period.

Sources indicate that the TTWO spike shows tokenized stocks can attract event-driven trading on-chain, comparable to some of the largest names in the segment. It also coincides with growing regulatory scrutiny of how tokenized stocks are supervised.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin (BTC) bull and SkyBridge Capital founder Anthony Scaramucci has argued that the world's biggest cryptocurrency could find a critical bottom as soon as this week.

Scaramucci's comments follow the leading cryptocurrency's struggle to recover from a catastrophic crypto market crash that took BTC to its lowest price level in over two years.

In the latest episode of All Things Markets on Nov. 20, the SkyBridge Capital founder joined Galaxy Digital CEO Mike Novogratz to discuss a potential bottom for Bitcoin.

Scaramucci shared his view that Bitcoin could see its bottom on Nov. 25, citing the cryptocurrency's four-year halving cycle as the driving force behind his comments.

"Before we came on, I asked ChatGPT when's the expected halving for Bitcoin," Scaramucci explained.

"And then when are we 500 days out from that halving? And the estimate was November 25th," he added.

This prediction stems from the idea that Bitcoin's price trends could follow a predictable four-year cycle that coincides with the cryptocurrency's halving events, when the newly introduced BTC supply is cut in half.

This theory suggests that Bitcoin could find its major bottom around the 500-day mark before its next halving, expected in 2028.

However, these theories are by no means a certainty when it comes to predicting future price action, especially with the current level of institutional participation and macroeconomic forces impacting the crypto market to an unprecedented extent.

During the conversation, Novogratz also took note of Bitcoin's history of forming double bottoms during its four-year cycles.

"And every four years, Bitcoin double bottomed," Novogratz remarked.

At the time, the Galaxy Digital CEO's comments suggested a potentially positive scenario, as Bitcoin had been able to hold its psychological $60,000 price level.

"If it doesn't break 60, that could be a good sign," he noted.

Unfortunately for Bitcoin, the cryptocurrency subsequently crashed below this critical price point. This has left some wondering whether the cryptocurrency has already found its ultimate bottom.

During the same conversation, Novogratz suggested that Bitcoin's short-term outlook could largely depend on the current situation in the stock market.

Specifically, the billionaire mentioned that a rebound in tech stocks could lead to a strong rally in Bitcoin's price.

In a recent development, "If we put in a bottom in the next couple days in the S&P here, down 3% from here, down 5% from here. And we have a rally back up. Man, Bitcoin is going to rally hard with it," Novogratz predicted.

However, he also warned that Bitcoin could see a lot of market-driven movements going forward, as opposed to crypto-specific movements.

"I think we're going to be stuck tethered to general sentiment and risk," he remarked.

Novogratz also believes that Bitcoin could trade in a range between $60,000 and $75,000 before a breakout or breakdown becomes apparent.

It has been revealed that bitcoin plunged to around $55,100 on Nov. 21, its lowest price level since September 2024, following another severe wave of sell-offs in the crypto market.

It then bounced back strongly to climb above $60,000 again, albeit briefly, before falling back to around $59,000 on Nov. 22.

The decline comes amid a serious price correction and increased pressure on the cryptocurrency market. Selling pressure remains high, and the declining number of users is not helping the price.

According to recent reports, XRPScan's data revealed 250,000 people 24 hours ago, while today's reading indicates barely 92,000 users. While the drop is significant, it should not be considered critical on its own. The decline partly reflects a regular weekend slowdown, when traders are generally less active, but it comes alongside the price correction and broader selling pressure.

It has been revealed that the highest point for this metric in November was 300,000, with a monthly average of approximately 200,000 active users. The number of users is a critical metric for the network's health, and a decline toward 100,000 often comes before bullish sentiment among investors. The current drop does not guarantee that sentiment will turn, especially as the price remains under pressure.

Apart from the negative on-chain trend, XRP's price performance has also been weak. The price lost roughly 5% from its November 19 close and even fell below the $0.90 price level, which was expected to serve as a foundation for recovery. XRP was around $0.915 on November 22 after closing at $0.9604 three days earlier.

The trend remains bearish, and the decline could become significantly worse.

Industry observers note that few expected a surge in market liquidations so soon, as Bitcoin fell below the $60,000 price level. XRP and other altcoins followed the broader market trend and suffered serious losses.

Interest in the network appears to be weakening as the price correction continues, so this drop in activity is not helping XRP's recovery.

A potential recovery above $0.9 could be the key to a quick rebound. However, the overall trend remains bearish and is unlikely to change unless significant market events occur.

Cycling Taught Me How to Suffer—a Lesson That Helped Me Lose 140 Pounds and Find Recovery

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1788 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that SEPTEMBER 2026, THE week of the UCI Road World Championships in Montreal and the city was lousy with bicycles.
  • Industry observers note that I'd heard elite cyclists—guys like Toms Skujins, Sean Quinn, and Mike Woods—talk about this pain in passing, but I was in Montreal to learn more.
  • Sources indicate that IN 2001, I was an obese drug addict.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that SEPTEMBER 2026, THE week of the UCI Road World Championships in Montreal and the city was lousy with bicycles. On most corners, a newly introduced pack of amateur cyclists gathered. Bixi—Montreal’s bike share program—was represented, but as a garnish to the inundation of mountain, beach, fixie, and road bikes, along with their riders from around the world, taking over the city. I watched all this in awe. Cycling changed me because it taught me how to suffer. The sport familiarized me with the type of suffering that wrecks you, but you put yourself through it on purpose. You suffer to emerge resilient and better.

Industry observers note that I'd heard elite cyclists—guys like Toms Skujins, Sean Quinn, and Mike Woods—talk about this pain in passing, but I was in Montreal to learn more. I wanted to know if they saw the power of suffering in the same way I did.

Sources indicate that IN 2001, I was an obese drug addict. Checking into rehab that year put a number to my weight: 536 pounds. I’d been diagnosed with congestive heart failure, drugs were quickly killing me, and I was motivated to change. Once I’d been sober for a year, I was able to see that my weight was causing me suffering.

According to recent reports, standing was a herculean effort, placing my feet in the right spot to support me, calculating the angle my knees would be in at the apex of my shifting mass, deep breath, locked core, and a hope and a prayer that I didn’t topple. Tying my shoes was done in bursts of held breath and near-blackouts. I slept sitting up, because the pressure of my chest caused me to choke and gasp. I could once soothe that suffering with food and drugs and kick that discomfort down the road a bit, but in sobriety I needed healthy outlets.

I’d successfully managed lose 100 pounds before my wife tricked me into going to the gym. When she’d ask that I go, I’d tell her that the gym was a place for fit people. So she bought me a package with a personal trainer, said I could flake on the appointments, but I’d be flushing money down the toilet if I did. I went, but I was geared towards avoidance, and whenever something in the gym got hard, I’d just tell the trainer I couldn’t do it.

In a recent development, riding a bike was something I did during outings with my wife and little kids maybe a few times a year. We’d cram our minivan full of bikes, find the flattest part of the Venice bike path, and slowly cruise for ten minutes at a time. Getting them back into the car was the hardest thing I had to work through.

Little did I know that someday cycling would be the key to changing my life.

Sources indicate that ROUND AND ROUND I went losing and regaining weight. In 2009, after getting down to 300 pounds and ballooning back up to over 400, faced with having to start over once again, I turned my sights to running.

Industry observers note that I tried running on a desolate stretch of the LA river near my house in Studio City. Not only was I unbearably slow, running hurt. My flat feet sent electric jolts of white-hot pain cascading up and through my body. That first day, I’d wrapped my ankles so tightly with ace bandages that my toes went numb. My feet were no better off and my nipples bled. The next day I could barely stand. The suffering didn’t stop when I stopped running. My feet, ankles, knees, and hips hurt long after—and I had no control over it.

With running out, but I turned to an old beach cruiser in our shed. The street we lived on was relatively flat, but every street branching off it was a steep climb. After a few rounds on my street, I decided to be ballsy and see how long I could last going uphill.

Sources indicate that my legs were screaming, but there was no electric jolt of pain in my pedal stroke. My heart thundered, my mind told me I had to stop. But without the jarring jolt I got when my feet hit the ground while running, I knew I could go further.

In a recent development, despite never riding my bike uphill as a kid, despite weighing 400 pounds, despite every physical and mental signal in me telling me to quit, I made it up to the top of that hill, up to Mulholland and Laurel Canyon, and it was glorious. Fighting through that urge to stop was incredible; getting to the top even more so. The pain while running was a warning that stayed with me after I stopped. The pain of cycling uphill was legs, lungs, and heart. I could push through it, and it stopped when I stopped.

Recent findings suggest that I asked Tour de France cyclist Mike Woods about this distinction of suffering when I was in Montreal. “Suffering is a bit of a misnomer for endurance events. Are you really suffering? It’s elected, you know?” he told me. “You choose the pain, you choose when to stop, you choose when to keep going. I don’t truly suffer. Suffering is when you don’t choose for that pain to be inflicted on you”.

Sources indicate that and then he said something that really resonated with me: “But it does prepare you for real suffering, when you have something bad happen to you in life. Doing endurance events, I find—it’s fake suffering, but when you have those bad moments in your life, you’re better prepared to manage them.”.

In a recent development, AFTER THAT HILL climb, I started riding my bike regularly, eventually graduated to a mountain bike, and then to a road bike. I rode to the top of every mountain in Los Angeles. I discovered I was capable of so much more than my mind or body allowed me to believe. Legs screaming, heart pounding, mind numbing, this was suffering, and I found that I loved it. And, like Woods noted, I found that the more I suffered on a bicycle, the less I suffered off it.

“One day at a time, one pedal stroke at a time. Just move forward,” Toms Skujins, a two-time Latvian road race champion, told me in Montreal. “When you’re racing, you can stop at any point. You’re the one doing the damage, you know? That’s very voluntary suffering, because there’s, obviously, things in the world that happen where you don’t choose to suffer, and you have no choice there. Here… if your legs are screaming too much, you can just stop. For me, that kind of suffering is definitely easier to take.”.

Sources indicate that within my first year of cycling, I was riding every day. There was a loop that took me from Studio City over the hill to West Hollywood. I’d cross Los Angeles, ride up PCH, cross the Santa Monica Mountains, and ride back to Studio City along Ventura Boulevard. It got me 100 miles and 8,000 feet of climbing, and I did it a few times a week. I’d do shorter 30- to 50-mile rides on the remaining days.

Sources indicate that sean Quinn, a US pro cyclist, gets it: “It sounds easy when you’re sitting on the couch, but when you’re actually in that moment suffering, your body’s basically sending you all the signals it can to make you just do anything else, just stop, stop the suffering,” he told me. “There’s no instant fix to a lot of your suffering. You have to be patient, accept that it’s gonna be shitty for a while, and wait it out, and keep a cool head, and eventually it does get better. Of course, you have to take action.”.

When I was riding every day, I got down to 213 pounds. I’d like to say I stayed there. But I went back to work, stopped riding, my diet unraveled, and over the next few years, I gained nearly all of it back.

In 2016, 400 pounds again, I ruptured the biceps tendon in my right arm and had to have surgery to repair it. As a sober guy, I turned down the post-op painkillers. I was up all night in pain and had to work the following day. On set, with the motion of production buzzing around me, the pain was dull, but it was unrelenting, just like a ride up Angeles Crest Highway, more than 120 miles out-and-back, with over 13,000 feet of elevation gain. I hadn’t chosen the injury, but I had chosen to go without the pills, and that reminded me of the pain on the bike, something I picked and something I knew would come to an end. I’d remind myself of that and go back to learning my lines and preparing for the scene.

It has been revealed that that day reminded me that I knew how to do this. So I got back on a diet, and by 2018 I was down to 260, and I’ve held steady there ever since.

Riding a bike taught me that I could suffer now in benefit of tomorrow. It’s been the most powerful lesson I’ve learned about myself.

ON THE DAY of the elite men’s road race, we fans lined the streets. There was dedicated bike parking near the finish line—Fans Village Bonjour Montreal—with thousands of bikes in neat rows. We all lined up to watch the attacks, riders going solo for that long and treacherous circuit. An American, Brandon McNulty, went off the front with about three laps to go and won the World Championship this year. It was thrilling to see. At the press conference afterward he said, “I was just dying, but I kept pushing.”.

Leaving Canada, I couldn’t help but think that I shared something with everyone else there for the races. A secret membership, dues paid in sweat, and a code, to respect and revel in my voluntary suffering.

I’d gone to Montreal to ask the riders if they saw suffering the way I did, and in different words, all three told me that what you do on the bike carries over into the rest of your life. I’d thought cycling taught me how to suffer, but what it did was give me a place where I was in control of it, where I could make it a practice, so that when the suffering of life came along, the suffering I had no control over, I was better equipped to deal with it.
